title: VALESKA Began with the Work
description: VALESKA began with a conviction: enterprise knowledge should follow the work that creates value and remain under the organization’s control.
body:
Today, VALESKA is being shaped as a governed knowledge layer for people and AI systems. It is intended to help an agent find the right evidence, understand where that evidence came from, respect who is allowed to use it, and carry forward decisions without treating every document as an isolated fragment.

The present goal is larger than recording individual documents or agent interactions. VALESKA is intended to ingest and model an organization’s operating verticals: its processes, systems, records, decisions, procedures, current work, and human and agent interactions. Each vertical becomes a governed corporate corpus that can support retrieval, evaluation, and selectively approved training for an on-premises system. The objective is to preserve the company’s alpha: its proprietary methods, operational history, relationships, and decision context.

That direction resembles the Palantir Sovereign AI Operating System Reference Architecture developed with NVIDIA, which grounds open models in an operational ontology and can run on cloud or on-premises infrastructure. VALESKA is its own architecture, but it shares a premise: an organization’s data, work, and accumulated decisions can become protected operational intelligence rather than material exported to a distant platform.

That description uses the language of the current moment: embeddings, retrieval, agents, provenance, permissions, and institutional memory. But the central idea is much older. VALESKA did not begin as an AI project. It began with a question about work.

Knowledge must follow the work that creates value

In 2004, while working at Northrop Grumman, I encountered value-stream thinking in manufacturing. A value stream makes visible the connected activities that turn an input into something useful for a customer. It exposes handoffs, waits, rework, responsibilities, and the places where a process loses momentum.

I began to wonder why enterprise content management was normally organized in a completely different way. Documents were usually arranged by department, by an abstract subject taxonomy, or by the habits of the people who created folders. Those structures might be familiar, but they did not describe how the organization actually produced value.

In a manufacturing setting, a value stream connects the work across functions. A customer need may pass through engineering, sourcing, production, quality, delivery, and support. The work is connected even when the reporting hierarchy is not. I believed the same principle could apply to enterprise knowledge: the information used to do the work should be organized around the process and value stream that produced it.

That was the beginning of what became the Value Stream Knowledge Architecture, which is now known as VALESKA.

From enterprise content management to knowledge architecture

The idea was not simply to redraw a folder tree. A process-centered architecture changes what information means inside an organization. A document becomes an artifact of work: an input, a decision, a handoff, a control, a reusable method, or evidence of an outcome. Its position should help a person understand what it is for, who uses it, and what comes before and after it.

I presented the concept at Northrop Grumman as a way to connect value-stream analysis and enterprise content management. It asked for a substantial change in how people thought about information, ownership, and structure. At the time, the proposal was too radical to become the organization’s operating model. The idea, however, was not abandoned. I continued developing it independently.

The early VALESKA materials focused on several practical requirements. Knowledge had to make tacit experience more explicit and reusable. A controlled vocabulary had to name the recurring parts of work consistently. Process structures had to be repeatable rather than rebuilt as one-off folder systems. Security had to align with the teams and responsibilities involved in the work. And the architecture had to be installable and maintainable, not merely illustrated in a diagram.

Those are still familiar problems. Anyone who has tried to find the authoritative version of a policy, reconstruct why a decision was made, or give an AI system safe access to organizational information has encountered them.

Architexturizer: making the idea executable

As the architecture took shape, I wrote Architexturizer in C++. Its purpose was to move the work beyond a paper model and toward an executable system. The name reflected the task: give an architecture enough structure that it could be constructed, applied, and used.

The program belonged to an era when a design like this had to carry much more of its intelligence in explicit rules, structures, and software logic. The ideas were coalescing: process models, controlled vocabularies, structured metadata, and the beginnings of semantic approaches to information. Yet implementation remained difficult. The available search technologies could match words and fields, but they could not reliably recognize the meaning of a question, retrieve the right context from a large body of material, or reason across relationships without extensive hand-built logic.

That limitation matters because VALESKA was never only about finding documents. It was about making knowledge usable in the context of work. A search result without purpose, authority, relationship, or history is often only a more quickly discovered fragment.

What changed

Embeddings and large language models changed the practical boundary. Information can now be represented and retrieved by meaning as well as by literal terminology. Language models can help interpret a question, synthesize evidence, and work through a structured task. Agent workflows can coordinate tools and steps that once had to be manually stitched together.

Those capabilities do not replace architecture. They make architecture more necessary. A capable model still needs to know which source is current, whether a claim is evidence or inference, what context surrounds a record, and whether the person or agent asking has permission to see it. Without those conditions, an AI system can be fluent while being unreliable.

That is why present-day VALESKA combines semantic retrieval with provenance, lineage, permissions, structured records, document trees, tables, relationships, and decision history. The system is evolving from an information model into a governed environment where human and agent work can share a durable memory.

The thread that connects the whole story

The technology has changed dramatically since the first value-stream insight. The underlying question has not: how should an organization preserve and use what it learns while doing its work?

VALESKA’s answer begins with the work itself. Build the knowledge structure around the value that work creates. Preserve the context that gives information meaning. Make the architecture explicit enough to govern, improve, and eventually allow intelligent systems to use responsibly.

This is the first post in a series tracing that evolution: from value-stream thinking, through Architexturizer and early knowledge-management practice, to the governed agent memory now taking shape.

Source note: This account draws on David Gargan’s firsthand experience and early VALESKA working materials. The historical series will distinguish founder account, contemporaneous documents, and recovered source-code artifacts as the archive is assembled.
